gist: Volts host David Roberts asks PG&E innovation lead Quinn Nakayama and Microsoft energy go-to-market leader Hannah Green why US utilities spend only ~0.2% of revenue on R&D despite surging data-center-driven demand and a ~40% rise in residential rates since 2021; they trace the innovation gap to capex-favoring rate regulation, immature digital/data infrastructure, multi-year pilot-to-scale failure, and organizational structure, while pointing to California's EPIC R&D fund and proposed multi-utility 'advanced market commitment' coalitions as emerging fixes.

insights.claim: Grid-enhancing technologies like dynamic line rating are widely deployed in Europe but remain a rounding error in the US mainly because of how different regulatory markets value distributed energy resources across system, transmission, and distribution views, not because the technology itself doesn't work.
insights.speaker: Quinn Nakayama, PG&E innovation lead
insights.so_what: Investors backing grid-enhancing-technology vendors should target markets with resolved DER value-stacking regulatory frameworks (e.g., California) rather than assume a uniform US-wide addressable market.
insights.quote: It's more of how does each regulatory market perceive the value of distributed energy resources across its entire sector from the system view versus transmission view versus distribution view.

insights.claim: PG&E already captures much of dynamic line rating's benefit through existing 'ambient adjusted ratings,' so for California utilities DLR functions as an incremental wind- and temperature-measurement refinement rather than a novel capability, which dampens urgency to adopt third-party DLR products even at an otherwise advanced utility.
insights.speaker: Quinn Nakayama, PG&E innovation lead
insights.so_what: DLR vendors should not assume uniform greenfield demand even among utilities widely seen as innovation leaders.
insights.quote: dynamic line rating from our perspective just is a wind measurement tool and a much more granular temperature measurement tool.

insights.claim: Most US utilities had flat or negative load growth for years, removing the incentive to adopt capacity-expanding grid technologies, and only the recent data-center- and EV-driven demand surge has made rapid adoption urgent.
insights.speaker: Quinn Nakayama, PG&E innovation lead
insights.so_what: The addressable market for grid-capacity technologies (DLR, advanced conductors, power flow controllers) has structurally expanded only in the last few years, implying a genuine adoption inflection ahead for pipeline vendors.
insights.quote: Most United States utilities across the board had flat in some areas negative load growth.

insights.claim: Digital grid controls software has matured faster in the global retail/behind-the-meter power sector than in traditional transmission-and-distribution utilities, because hybrid power plants and complex distributed generation created earlier technical need in that segment.
insights.speaker: Hannah Green, Microsoft energy go-to-market lead
insights.so_what: Grid-controls software vendors may find faster near-term revenue in retail/independent-power-producer segments than in regulated T&D utilities.
insights.quote: the retail sector globally has matured it much much faster than say you know traditional TND utilities

themes.theme: Pilot-program hell and the product-development mindset

insights.claim: Roughly 70% of surveyed utility-tech startups say they land a pilot with a utility, but pilots routinely fail to convert into scaled programs because utilities treat pilots as isolated tests rather than iterative product-development partnerships.
insights.speaker: host, citing an industry study
insights.so_what: Investors evaluating grid-tech startups should treat a signed utility pilot as a weak signal and instead track conversion-to-scale rates.
insights.quote: something like 70% of the startups they surveyed said yeah we were able to get a pilot from out of utilities but very often that's just where things stay.

insights.claim: Vendor technology typically arrives at a utility only 60-70% 'baked,' and closing that gap requires the utility to commit its subject-matter expertise and proprietary data to co-develop the product, not just test it and issue a pass/fail verdict.
insights.speaker: Quinn Nakayama, PG&E innovation lead
insights.so_what: Grid-tech startups that build real co-development processes with utility subject-matter experts will convert pilots to scaled programs at a much higher rate than those pitching plug-and-play claims.
insights.quote: technologies typically are around 70% 60% 70% baked and what is required is the utility subject matter expertise and our data to be able to then work with these companies to modify their products

insights.claim: Treating an AI or innovation initiative as a 'bolt-on' side project rather than embedding it in a company's core strategy is a self-fulfilling trap that keeps pilots from ever scaling.
insights.speaker: Hannah Green, Microsoft energy go-to-market lead
insights.so_what: Investors assessing utility AI vendors should check whether the utility counterpart has embedded the initiative into core, KPI-linked strategy, since that is a leading indicator of scale-up odds.
insights.quote: you fall into a trap that becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy of making it a bolt-on.

insights.claim: Most deployed smart meters ('AMI 1.0') function like basic flip phones — reading consumption and occasionally voltage — and cannot support the app-like analytics layer needed for household- or microgrid-level optimization, even though private products exist that could exploit richer meter data.
insights.speaker: Quinn Nakayama, PG&E innovation lead
insights.so_what: The addressable market for smart-meter-data analytics software is gated by the pace of AMI 2.0 hardware refresh cycles, not by underlying data availability.
insights.quote: a lot of the smart meters that are out there are your what I would consider your flip phone type of smart meters

insights.claim: PG&E is rolling out 'AMI 2.0' meters that measure voltage at roughly 32 kHz resolution and support app-like extensibility, but only a handful of US utilities have undertaken wide-scale rollouts of this next-generation metering so far.
insights.speaker: Quinn Nakayama, PG&E innovation lead
insights.so_what: Grid-analytics vendors dependent on granular, sub-second meter data have a narrow near-term set of addressable utility customers, PG&E among a small handful of peers.
insights.quote: name me how many utilities have widescale roll out of AMI 2.0 and I can count them on my hand.

insights.claim: The utility sector generates data volumes rivaled by few industries besides healthcare, but the binding constraint isn't data quantity — it's whether that data is clean, usable, and converted into actionable insight rather than more control-room alarms.
insights.speaker: Hannah Green, Microsoft energy go-to-market lead
insights.so_what: AI and data vendors should lead utility pitches with data-cleaning and insight-generation value rather than more raw data collection.
insights.quote: there's not a utility out there that necessarily needs more data, but do we have that data in a clean and usable format?

insights.claim: Utilities historically never needed to track which phase of the secondary/primary distribution system a given asset sat on, because the system could balance without it; rising two-way power flow from solar and EVs now makes that missing data a real operational gap.
insights.speaker: Hannah Green, Microsoft energy go-to-market lead
insights.so_what: Distribution-grid data-mapping and digital-twin vendors are addressing a genuine, newly-created data gap tied to DER growth, not a legacy oversight now being cosmetically patched.
insights.quote: no utility had to really record that because you could get things to balance generally on the system and you were fine.

themes.theme: The five pillars and stage-gate funnel of utility innovation

insights.claim: Effective utility innovation requires five aligned elements — strategy, structure, people, process, and technology — and missing any one undermines the rest; strategy (tying innovation to top-level KPIs like reliability and affordability) is the foundation that secures organizational buy-in.
insights.speaker: Quinn Nakayama, PG&E innovation lead
insights.so_what: Investors or partners evaluating a utility's innovation readiness can use this five-part checklist as a due-diligence framework rather than judging on technology adoption alone.
insights.quote: You need to have strategy, structure, people, process, and technology. If you don't have those five things lined up, things never going to work.

insights.claim: Utilities that run a formal innovation funnel move ideas through ideate, incubate, accelerate, and scale stages, with a roughly 90%+ kill rate expected at the ideation stage alone.
insights.speaker: Quinn Nakayama, PG&E innovation lead
insights.so_what: Startups pitching utilities should expect and design around a formal, high-attrition stage-gate process rather than a single yes/no evaluation.
insights.quote: Your no rate should be at least 90% or greater of every single idea that comes across your desk

insights.claim: The 'scale' stage is the hardest for utility innovation because every functional area already considers its budget underfunded, so a new technology must show payback within a single fiscal year to win budget owners' buy-in.
insights.speaker: Quinn Nakayama, PG&E innovation lead
insights.so_what: Vendors should engineer pilot economics to demonstrate sub-one-year payback, since that is the actual gating criterion for utility budget approval, not just technical performance.
insights.quote: every single functional area is feels like they're 30% to 50% underfunded.

insights.claim: A powerful internal-sales framing is to pitch innovation projects as the mechanism to close the 'gap to target' between multi-year corporate KPI goals and the budget actually allocated to hit them, which secures executive buy-in more effectively than pitching innovation on its own abstract merits.
insights.speaker: Quinn Nakayama, PG&E innovation lead
insights.so_what: Internal champions and vendor sales teams should frame proposals around closing red/amber KPI gaps rather than pitching innovation as a standalone value proposition.
insights.quote: you're going to have gaps to targets. Great. That is where innovation and technology lives

themes.theme: Build vs. buy vs. partner, and vendor-sprawl security risk

insights.claim: Enterprise-scale software rollout to tens of thousands of utility employees is a distinct and difficult skill set from prototyping, so utilities must decide deliberately what to build in-house versus buy versus co-develop with a small set of strategic partners.
insights.speaker: Hannah Green, Microsoft energy go-to-market lead
insights.so_what: Vendors should position around the enterprise-deployment gap (security, scale, reliability) rather than compete on prototype capability alone, since AI has commoditized initial build speed.
insights.quote: there's a big difference between vibe coding something and rolling it out to 45,000 people securely over time.

insights.claim: Utility CIOs face an unsustainable integration cost ceiling from vendor sprawl — too many point-solution startups create unmanageable data flows and APIs — which pushes utilities to route smaller vendors through large incumbent platform partners like Schneider Electric, SAP, and Oracle as a matchmaking layer instead of contracting with startups directly.
insights.speaker: Quinn Nakayama, PG&E innovation lead
insights.so_what: Early-stage grid-tech startups may find faster distribution by embedding as modules within large platform incumbents than by selling directly to utility CIOs.
insights.quote: if you start to have a thousand applications that you're working with on all these related startups, you have data flying everywhere.

insights.claim: A widespread but under-discussed AI security risk in utilities is 'shadow AI': employees increasingly use unsanctioned consumer AI tools to get work done because the enterprise hasn't rolled out sanctioned tools broadly, creating IP, PII, and operational-data leakage risk at organizations that run the grid.
insights.speaker: Hannah Green, Microsoft energy go-to-market lead
insights.so_what: A utility's AI-related cyber risk should be assessed by the breadth of its sanctioned AI-tool rollout, not just perimeter security; narrow rollouts (e.g., to a few hundred of 40,000 employees) leave shadow-AI exposure.
insights.quote: The number of people using unsanctioned AI at work is like stayed the same because people are doing it.

insights.claim: Business models where a vendor ingests a utility's operational data and returns AI-driven insights constitute a form of data leakage of IP and PII, and utilities should be skeptical of vendors that use customer data to train their own models outside the client's protected environment.
insights.speaker: Hannah Green, Microsoft energy go-to-market lead
insights.so_what: Due diligence on AI/grid-software vendors should specifically probe whether customer data is used to train the vendor's models outside the client's own environment.
insights.quote: your data is your data is your data.

insights.claim: A robust partner ecosystem spanning core-systems vendors, platform providers, and innovation co-developers does not reduce a utility's need for strong internal technology and innovation talent — the two grow together rather than substituting for one another.
insights.speaker: Hannah Green, Microsoft energy go-to-market lead
insights.so_what: Investors should not assume growing utility reliance on vendors like Microsoft displaces internal utility tech hiring, moderating fears of vendor-capture risk.
insights.quote: I don't think any part of that ecosystem reduces the need for you to have a great set of in-house technology and innovation talent.

themes.theme: AI adoption pace, shadow risk, and human-in-the-loop for critical infrastructure

insights.claim: Traditional utility technology projects follow a rigid 5-to-7-year 'big block' implementation cycle (plan, deploy, run), but AI-era development is shifting toward continuous, iterative 'little loops' spanning multiple concurrent AI models and agents integrated into large existing processes.
insights.speaker: Hannah Green, Microsoft energy go-to-market lead
insights.so_what: AI-focused grid software vendors should position offerings around continuous iteration rather than the discrete RFP-to-deployment cycle utilities are used to budgeting for.
insights.quote: where we're seeing this shift with AI it's going to look a lot more like a bunch of little loops

insights.claim: The electric utility industry has already used AI for roughly 20 years (e.g., in forecasting and asset monitoring); what's new is not AI's presence in the sector but the accelerating pace at which the underlying technology itself is evolving.
insights.speaker: Hannah Green, Microsoft energy go-to-market lead
insights.so_what: Investors should distinguish long-established 'AI in utilities' as a mature category from the current wave of generative/agentic AI, a distinct and faster-moving sub-opportunity.
insights.quote: our industry has been using AI for 20 years.

insights.claim: Microsoft's utility AI approach is explicitly 'human-led' — AI augments human capacity and can support automated processes, but fully automated decision-making without human oversight is treated as a distinct, more advanced future state not appropriate for core grid infrastructure today.
insights.speaker: Hannah Green, Microsoft energy go-to-market lead
insights.so_what: Vendors marketing 'full automation' for core utility operations are likely ahead of what utilities and regulators will actually accept in the near term.
insights.quote: we are very much AI enabled, human le operator.

insights.claim: In AI-driven asset-health monitoring, false positives overload maintenance programs while false negatives leave real asset failures undetected, so utilities require human review of AI outputs until model error rates are proven low enough to remove that check.
insights.speaker: Quinn Nakayama, PG&E innovation lead
insights.so_what: AI-for-asset-management vendors will be adopted incrementally with human-in-the-loop gating, extending sales cycles for any full-automation claims.
insights.quote: if you have a whole bunch of false positives, your maintenance program is going to be underwater. If you have a whole bunch of false negatives, you're not aware of potential asset failures that may be occurring.

insights.claim: The Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) launched an initiative this week called 'Safer AI Power' to build shared frameworks and risk-assessment methodology for sensitive AI use cases in utility infrastructure, backed early by Microsoft, so individual utilities don't have to independently reinvent AI risk assessment.
insights.speaker: Hannah Green, Microsoft energy go-to-market lead
insights.so_what: A shared industry risk framework from EPRI could lower individual utilities' AI-adoption friction and compress sales cycles for AI vendors targeting core infrastructure use cases.
insights.quote: what they announced just this week with safer AI. Power, this is an initiative to actually work through AI use cases that might be more sensitive

themes.theme: Capex bias and utility funding mechanisms

insights.claim: Most utility R&D spending gets folded into the operations-and-management budget and must be recovered via a rate case, whereas California's EPIC (Electric Program Investment Charge) — a commission-mandated, ratepayer-funded pot dedicated solely to R&D — has been the real catalyst enabling California utilities to innovate since 2011 across four completed funding cycles, with a fifth upcoming.
insights.speaker: Quinn Nakayama, PG&E innovation lead
insights.so_what: Grid-tech investors should treat regulatory-mandated dedicated R&D funding mechanisms like EPIC as a structural enabler, and use their presence or absence as a state-level market-attractiveness signal.
insights.quote: since 2011, we've had four cycles of this. We're about to go into our fifth cycle.

insights.claim: PG&E justifies its EPIC-funded R&D internally by demonstrating concrete bill-savings ROI, citing an example of turning roughly $50 million of R&D funding into an estimated $150-200 million of customer savings.
insights.speaker: Quinn Nakayama, PG&E innovation lead
insights.so_what: Vendors seeking utility R&D-budget-funded pilots should quantify bill-savings ROI multiples, not just technical KPIs, to secure continued funding.
insights.quote: if I get $50 million, can I turn it into 150 $200 million worth of savings?

insights.claim: Because capital projects earn a guaranteed rate of return recovered gradually over decades (e.g., a $300 million project amortized over 40 years) while O&M expenses hit ratepayers the following year, utility rate-making structurally biases utilities toward capex-heavy solutions and away from cheaper opex/software alternatives.
insights.speaker: Quinn Nakayama, PG&E innovation lead
insights.so_what: This capex-vs-opex asymmetry is the core regulatory mechanism explaining why utilities favor pole-and-wire spending over cheaper software/digital solutions, constraining the realistic addressable market for cost-saving software pitches.
insights.quote: A capital project that's $300 million that's spread over 40 years hits the rateayer much less over a long period of time.

insights.claim: Many utility executives outside California remain eager to maximize capex spending on data-center-driven infrastructure build-out and have not yet fully internalized the political blowback from a roughly 40% rise in residential electricity rates since 2021.
insights.speaker: Hannah Green, Microsoft energy go-to-market lead
insights.so_what: Investors modeling utility capex trajectories should watch for capital discipline to lag rate-case political risk in the near term rather than assume immediate self-correction.
insights.quote: I see utility executives just like drunk on this.

insights.claim: A practical workaround to the capex-bias problem is reclassifying some O&M-style expenses to be spread ('peanut-buttered') across a longer time horizon, so they resemble capital treatment and hit ratepayers less abruptly in a single year, rather than waiting for wholesale reform of rate-of-return regulation.
insights.speaker: Quinn Nakayama, PG&E innovation lead
insights.so_what: Watch for utilities and regulators experimenting with amortized opex treatment as an interim fix to capex bias — a regulatory-innovation trend worth tracking.
insights.quote: operation and management related expenses and figure out how to peanut butter them a little bit more across a broader range of time, which smells like capital

insights.claim: The deeper fix to capex bias is reclassifying digital and software infrastructure itself as legitimate capex ('digital infrastructure,' not IT back-office), since the best use of a capital dollar may increasingly be a sensor or software system rather than a pole or wire.
insights.speaker: Hannah Green, Microsoft energy go-to-market lead
insights.so_what: A regulatory/accounting shift toward capitalizing digital and software spend would materially expand utilities' addressable capex budget for AI and software vendors.
insights.quote: infrastructure is no longer the best spend of a capital dollar may not be a pole or a wire or a sensor.

themes.theme: Coalition financing: advanced market commitments and 'kingmaker' utilities

insights.claim: Because no utility wants to be first mover on new technology, Quinn proposes EPRI-coordinated 'advanced market commitments' in which a lead ('kingmaker') utility co-develops and proves out a technology while 7-10 other utilities pre-commit non-binding purchase amounts (e.g., $10 million each), aggregating to roughly $70-100 million in signaled demand for VCs and startups.
insights.speaker: Quinn Nakayama, PG&E innovation lead
insights.so_what: Watch for EPRI-coordinated advanced market commitment structures as a new financing/de-risking mechanism that could compress venture timelines for grid-tech startups by pre-validating multi-utility demand.
insights.quote: You put, I don't know, 710 utilities together for that, you get a 70 million to $100 million type of advanced market commitment.

insights.claim: Quinn suggests utilities should specialize as 'kingmakers' on different technology categories aligned to their regional risk exposure — e.g., PG&E leading on wildfire, drone, and computer-vision technologies given California's wildfire risk, while other utilities lead on transmission technologies tied to data-center buildout — in exchange for preferential deal terms.
insights.speaker: Quinn Nakayama, PG&E innovation lead
insights.so_what: Startups can target sector-leading 'kingmaker' utilities aligned to their specific use case as anchor customers, since those utilities have both the risk exposure and coalition-building incentive to invest first.
insights.quote: We'll do drones and wildfire related technologies and computer vision and this other utility over here will do be the kingmaker on something else.

insights.claim: Utility sales cycles for grid-tech startups routinely run 3-5 years, and this pace often financially exhausts small vendors before they can scale past their first reference customer.
insights.speaker: Quinn Nakayama, PG&E innovation lead
insights.so_what: Investors in early-stage grid-tech startups should underwrite multi-year cash runway assumptions given empirically long utility sales cycles, independent of product quality.
insights.quote: the sales cycle in a utility is super long and it crushes some of these startups
